summary:
The anti-discrimination provision in force since 1 January 2007 makes anyone who publicly makes a statement threatening, insulting or degrading a group on account of race, colour, national or ethnic origin, religion or sexual orientation liable to a fine or up to two years' imprisonment. Gender identity is not among the listed grounds. On the sourced account this made the Faroe Islands the last Northern European jurisdiction to prohibit discrimination and harassment on grounds of sexual orientation.

Before that provision took effect, homophobic conduct was legally unaddressed. In 2006 the openly gay singer, songwriter and radio host Rasmus Rasmussen was severely beaten by five men in Tórshavn and hospitalised shortly after coming out; he and his family then received threatening telephone calls, and police refused to handle the case because no Faroese law banned discrimination against sexual minorities at the time. He was later moved to a psychiatric hospital with severe depression exacerbated by the beating, never recovered, and died by suicide in 2012. The most recent documented assault in this record is that 2006 attack; no later instance is documented.

A second documented attack dates from 2005, when the Norwegian drag group Great Garlic Girls had to run from a gang of young men intent on physically assaulting them in Tórshavn; the group was not attacked anywhere else on its tour.

Hostility from elected office is documented across a decade. In September 2010 Centre Party leader Jenis av Rana refused to attend a state banquet for the visiting Icelandic prime minister and her partner, citing his religion. In June 2015 Løgting Speaker Jógvan á Lakjuni published a letter attacking the national broadcaster Kringvarp Føroya for the space it gave LGBT Føroyar and condemning a drag show at the Nordic House as 'non-culture', asking whether 'these people do not feel any shame'. The same year av Rana demanded that Pride be banned and repeatedly compared LGBT Føroyar to Sea Shepherd whale-hunting protesters, and his party remains formally opposed to homosexuality. Singer Eivor Pálsdóttir publicly urged people to ignore him, documenting organised public pushback alongside the hostility.

Public expression has been contested since the first gay pride march in 2005, which provoked substantial controversy; in 2015 av Rana also suggested the Tórshavn pride parade be moved out of the city centre.

Partner recognition is unresolved in this record. In 2006 LGBT activists gathered around 20,000 online signatures demanding an end to sexual-orientation discrimination and a registered-partnership law aligned with the rest of the Nordics; at that point the Faroe Islands, with a population of about 47,000, had neither protection nor partnership recognition. No later sourced statement establishes the current status of partnership or marriage registration here.
tangentialFactors:
Public petitioning has run in both directions. An internet petition after the 2006 assault on Rasmus Rasmussen collected 20,000 signatures, and eight women in Tórshavn gathered a further 2,000 by email and in shops, tourist centres and gas stations. A petition against same-sex marriage gathered 1,262 signatures.

The record documents hostility to LGBT public expression alongside organised counter-mobilisation: singer Eivor Pálsdóttir publicly urged people to ignore Jenis av Rana's call to ban Pride in 2015.
localsOnly:
Same-sex sexual activity has been legal in the Faroe Islands since 1933, when it was decriminalised across the Kingdom of Denmark. The age of consent for male same-sex relations was set at 18 and stayed there until 1988, when the Løgting adopted a gender-neutral age of 15, eleven years after Denmark made that change.

Residents' protection machinery rests on the 1 January 2007 provision, which lists sexual orientation but not gender identity among its protected grounds. Police practice before that date is documented as refusing to handle a 2006 assault on those grounds; no later sourced account of police handling of anti-LGBT complaints appears in this record.

Political opposition is on the record: the Centre Party remains formally opposed to homosexuality, and its leader Jenis av Rana has campaigned against Pride since at least 2015.
outOfScopeNotes:
The current status of partnership or marriage registration in the Faroe Islands is unresolved in this record; the latest sourced statement on the question dates from 2006.

No sourced figure in this inventory measures current prevalence of violence against trans people in the Faroe Islands, and no trans-specific incident is documented; the two assaults recorded here are from 2005 and 2006.

Whether the 2007 provision has been used in any prosecution is not sourced here.
